title: Taiwan.traditionelle Handwerkskunst und immaterielles Kulturerbe: Anerkennung durch das System, aber keine Lehrlinge mehr
description: Im Dezember 2022 wurde der 87-jährige Su Qingliang aus Kaohsiung von dem Ministerium für Kultus und Bildung als „Menschliches Nationalliste“ ausgezeichnet; er starb sechs Monate später. Taiwan erst 2005 in dem „Gesetz zur Erhaltung von Kulturgütern“ den Abschnitt über „Techniken zur Erhaltung von Kulturgütern und ihre Bewahrer“ verankert, was 50 Jahre nach Japan und 43 Jahre nach Südkorea lag. Als das System endlich bereit war, war das Lehrlingsverhältnis bereits in den 1970er- und 1980er-Jahren durch die Industrialisierung und den Auslandsauftrag zusammengebrochen. Von über 600 traditionellen Handwerkern sind die Unter 50-Jährigen nur die Ausnahme. Je länger die Liste, desto weniger Menschen können noch unterrichten.

title: Taiwan''s "Dashcam" Society: The Aesthetics of Mass Surveillance, Technological Evolution, and Whistleblower Justice
description: Why are dashcams almost a "standard feature" in Taiwan''s cars and scooters? This is not just for legal defense; it has evolved into a unique digital landscape. From the dominance of the supply chain, regulatory loopholes, social friction among whistleblowers, to the reliance of news media on the "Three Tools," Taiwan is undergoing an experiment in citizen-participatory digital surveillance.

title: Taiwan''s Election Rally Culture and Stage Truck Aesthetics: A Sociological Observation from "Dong Suan" to Democratic Carnival
description: Every election, Taiwan's streets transform into a massive democratic theater. From the Transformers-like aesthetics of stage trucks and the smoky scent of democratic sausages to the legal threshold of a 30-dollar bento box, this unique election rally culture is not only a tool for political mobilization but also a profound microcosm of Taiwan's vernacular vitality and social change.

title: Taiwan''s Future Resolution: Two Characters, "Currently," Held Up for Twenty-Seven Years
description: In 1999, Lin I-hsiung added the two characters "currently" before "Republic of China," which displeased the Chen faction. These two characters simultaneously soothed hardliners and middle voters, opening the door for the first peaceful transfer of power in 2000. Twenty-seven years later, Taiwan''s young people take it for granted that "Taiwan has always been independent," unaware that this common sense comes from a document full of ambiguity.

title: Taiwan''s History of Going Abroad: An Island People''s Cross-Border Narrative from "Police Headquarters Approval" to "Worldwide Access"
description: On New Year's Day 1979, Taiwan issued its first tourist passport. This was more than the release of a piece of paper — it was a turning point from martial-law isolation to citizen diplomacy, documenting how Taiwanese people transformed from 'foreign-exchange-wasting' sinners into world travelers.

title: Taiwan''s Homophonic Taboo Culture: Why Does "Four" Cause Society to Skip Floors?
description: From the absence of the 4th floor in hospitals to the astronomical bidding for license plate "8888," Taiwan''s sensitivity to homophones is among the highest in the world.

title: Taiwan''s Power and Semiconductors: The Electricity Bill of the "Protector of the Nation"
description: Taiwan's international leverage in semiconductors is built upon a very concrete power system. Advanced fabs, EUV lithography, advanced packaging, AI server testing, and data centers all require stable, low-interruption, and scalable power. This article does not frame semiconductor electricity use as a mere environmental grievance, but places it back into the context of supply chain games: while the world needs Taiwan to manufacture AI chips, Taiwan must also address who bears the costs of electricity, carbon emissions, and energy security risks.

title: Taiwan's 16 Indigenous Peoples: A Cultural Map
description: "16" is not a naturally occurring number—it is the result of negotiation. From 210,000 Amis to 441 Kanakanavu, Taiwan''s indigenous peoples possess a cultural depth far exceeding any official roster.

title: Taiwan's 5G Network Construction and Digital Transformation
description: Tracing Taiwan's journey from leading in 4G to deploying 5G, exploring the national strategy for digital transformation and smart application development.

title: Taiwan's Age-Inclusive Travel and Living Culture: When Human Warmth Becomes the Strongest Barrier-Free Facility
description: Observing Taiwanese society from a family perspective, how it redefines the meaning of "traveling together as one family" on the path to an ultra-aged society through human warmth and inclusive facilities.

title: Taiwan's Agricultural Landscapes and Industrial Distribution
description: The transformation path of Taiwan, from "Taiwan''s Granary" to "High-Value Agriculture," showcased through the agricultural landscapes from north to south.

title: Taiwan's Agriculture and Rural Revitalization
description: From Rice Kingdom to Precision Agriculture: The Story of Agricultural Transformation and Rural Community Regeneration in Taiwan

title: Taiwan's AI Everyday — When Artificial Intelligence Enters the Streets and Alleyways
description: Taiwanese people interact with AI more than a dozen times a day, but most don't know they're talking to AI.

title: Taiwan's Animal Drug Controversy: Where an Island Treats Pets as Family but Pet Medicines as Commodities
description: On July 1, 2026, a new Taiwan regulation on human drugs used for companion animals is set to take effect. Of 701 approved drugs, only 144 have been registered. Medical oxygen: zero. 100,000+ pet owners have signed a petition to delay it. This is a ten-year legal gap traced back to a 2012 counterfeit drug case, a Pandora's box opened in 2022 by a legislator, and a first-ever conviction in 2024.

title: Taiwan's Animation Outsourcing Industry
description: Taiwan was once a global animation outsourcing powerhouse where companies like Cuckoos' Nest Studio handled classic Hollywood animations, producing one-third of global animation output at its peak.

title: Taiwan's Arcade Culture and Streetscapes
description: Corridors of shelter and life: memories of Taiwan's streets woven with scooters, street vendors, and human warmth

title: Taiwan's Art Education and College Development
description: The dual tracks of art education in Taiwan—the National Taiwan Normal University system (teacher training) and the professional art colleges (National Taipei University of the Arts, Southern Taiwan University of the Arts, National Taiwan University of the Arts)—are traced from the 1955 establishment of a national art school to the current landscape.

title: Taiwan's Artificial Intelligence Development and Future Strategy: The Hardware Ticket Is Secured, Where's the Next Battle?
description: On October 8, 2024, the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Hopfield and Hinton, and the next day, Chemistry went to AlphaFold's trio. On May 29 of the same year, Jensen Huang dined with Morris Chang at Taipei's Ningxia Night Market, sharing oyster omelets. Taiwan manufactures 90% of the world's AI servers and 72% of advanced wafers, yet it was absent from the 42-year-old neural network and 50-year protein folding solutions. From PTT founder Lucas Wang's Taiwan AI Labs to the Traditional Chinese LLM model TAIDE backed by Taiwan's National Science and Technology Council, is being just a contract manufacturer enough for this island?

title: Taiwan’s Assisted Reproduction: An Embryo Crosses Borders, But a Family Cannot Automatically Cross the Law
description: In 2020, female partners Mota and City traveled to Cambodia for IVF, spending approximately NT$2 million over four years. Taiwan enacted an Assisted Reproduction Act in 2007 and expanded IVF subsidies in 2021, but it was not until the 2025 legislative draft that unmarried women and married female same-sex couples were included. The technology is mature; the law is catching up not just to reproductive methods, but to who qualifies as a family.

title: Taiwan's Bus System: After Hsinchu Bus Drives Away, Who Will Pick Up the People Without Steering Wheels?
description: On the morning of September 15, 2024, at Tongluo Railway Station, more than 30 people, from kindergarten children to a 90-year-old elder, boarded the last Hsinchu Bus 5658 service. From Taipei's first joint-operation route in 1977, to rural areas left with only two services a day, drivers averaging 51 years old, and TPASS monthly passes driving Hualien ridership up by nearly 70 percent, buses have always carried people with no other choice: students commuting to school, older adults who do not drive, families without cars. And this system is being pulled out from under them, route by route.

title: Taiwan's Choirs: Sixty Years from Rongxing to Asia's Top Five
description: In 1957, Lu Quan-sheng and Gu Wei-fu founded the Rongxing Children's Chorus, transforming rustic folk tunes into refined choral arrangements. Over six decades later, the Taipei Philharmonic brought its own flag to the Hungarian stage, the Puli Junior High School Chorus achieved a three-peat as world champion, and the O-Kai Singers accumulated 55 international awards. From campus-wide participation to world-class professionalism, this choral excellence rests on a complete ecosystem — and on a history of choirs defending dignity under political suppression.

title: Taiwan's Circular Economy and Resource Recycling
description: Transitioning from a linear to a circular economy, exploring Taiwan's resource recycling, waste management, and sustainable development models

title: Taiwan's Climate
description: Annual rainfall 2.5 times the global average, yet ranked among the world's top 20 water-stressed nations — Taiwan's climate is never what you expect

title: Taiwan's Climate Crisis and Net-Zero Transition: The Choice of Physical Limits Began When the NMMC Referendum Failed
description: The August 23, 2025, referendum on extending the life of NMMC saw 4.34 million 'yes' votes, with 74% in favor, but a voter turnout of 29.53% did not meet the threshold. With the referendum failing, Lai Ching-te announced three principles the next day, and seven months later, Taipower submitted the life extension application to the Nuclear Safety Commission on March 27, 2026. With 98% of energy relying on imports, a NT$9 trillion net-zero goal, geothermal capacity only reaching 7.4 MW against a 200 MW target, offshore wind being ranked seventh globally in installed capacity, Onkalo's ultimate disposal site, and TerraPower's fourth-generation nuclear power—this island's energy issue has never been a political one; it is a matter of physical limits.

title: Taiwan's Coastal Topography and Marine Landscapes
description: On Earth, few places allow you to descend from a 4,000-meter mountain peak into a 7,500-meter deep trench in less than 150 kilometers. Taiwan can. The coastline of this island is an ongoing collision site—breathtakingly beautiful.

title: Taiwan's Coffee Culture: The Island Where Convenience Stores Sell 600 Million Cups a Year
description: The first coffee trees planted in Gukeng, Yunlin during the Japanese colonial period grew, a century later, into a cityscape with a café every fifty meters. Louisa Coffee has opened more than 600 locations — surpassing Starbucks. Alishan coffee has made its way into international competitions. For Taiwanese people, coffee has never been just coffee.

title: Taiwan's Community Universities: Turning Classrooms into Public Squares
description: From Wenshan's first community university to nationwide institutionalization, understanding how Taiwan transforms lifelong learning into a training ground for local governance and civic action.

title: Taiwan's Convenience Store Culture
description: A kingdom of convenience stores at the forefront of global density, where 7-Eleven and FamilyMart's localization innovations redefine modern lifestyles

title: Taiwan's COVID-19 Pandemic and Vaccines: The Eighteen Months That Were Bought, and the Shot That Came Too Late
description: On February 15, 2020, an unlicensed taxi driver who had never left Taiwan died in hospital — the country's first COVID-19 death. Through border controls and a National Health Insurance card, Taiwan kept the pandemic outside its doors for almost eighteen months, recording only 799 confirmed cases and 7 deaths in all of 2020. But the first vaccines didn't arrive until March 2021, and only 117,000 doses at that; when Omicron arrived in 2022, senior citizens' third doses still lagged behind. That year, the median age of death was 82 — ten years older than the year before. Several other groups who bore the cost — people whose compensation claims were denied, people who left hospitals, people confined to dormitories — have, in many cases, still not been counted in any statistic to this day.

title: Taiwan's Cram School Culture: The Rise and Fall of One Street, and an Entire Society's Anxiety Bill
description: In 1981, over 100,000 college retake students and 48 cram schools crowded into Nanyangstreet in Taipei. Forty years later only three remained, with fewer than 2,500 students, and the ground-floor storefronts had all become bubble tea shops. But cram schools didn't disappear — they moved into neighborhood alleys across the island, growing from 18,000 locations to more than there are convenience stores. Education reform promised to loosen things up; instead, the number of cram schools tripled.

title: Taiwan's Creator Economy: A Battlefield of 23 Million Fragmented Audiences
description: The market is under 1% the size of the US's, yet creators operate on twice as many platforms — how do Taiwan's creators survive?

title: Taiwan’s Democratic Transition: The Grave Dug by Authoritarianism
description: Every crackdown breeds more resistance. From the February 28 Incident to the Sunflower Movement, how an island allowed a dictatorial regime to cultivate the very forces that buried it.

title: Taiwan's Digital Imaging and Animation Industry
description: From a global powerhouse of animation outsourcing to a new force in original content: the half-century transformation of Taiwan's digital imaging industry.

title: Taiwan's diplomatic allies and international diplomacy: 12 allies, 113 missions, 177 visa-free countries (2026)
description: Nurral brach am 15. Januar 2024 die diplomatischen Beziehungen ab, nur 48 Stunden nach Lai Ching-te's Wahl zum Präsidenten, wodurch die Anzahl der diplomatischen Vertretungen von 13 auf 12 sank. Im selben Jahr hatte Taiwan 113 ausländische Botschaften, Reisepässe für 177 Länder und TSMC produzierte 90 % der fortschrittlichen Chips weltweit, während das Europäische Parlament mit 432:60:71 die Resolution 2758 der UN verabschiedete, die China kritisiert. Auf dem Papier schrumpft es, aber im Schatten expandiert es; ein Kampf um die Auslegung des internationalen Rechts kehrt sich um.

title: Taiwan’s Diplomatic Allies and International Diplomacy: 12 Allies, 113 Overseas Offices, Visa-Free Access to 177 Countries (2026)
description: On January 15, 2024, 48 hours after Lai Ching-te was elected president, Nauru announced the severance of diplomatic relations, reducing Taiwan’s diplomatic allies from 13 to 12. Yet that same year, Taiwan had 113 overseas offices, its passport provided access to 177 countries, TSMC produced 90% of the world’s advanced chips, and the European Parliament passed a resolution by 432:60:71 opposing China’s distortion of UN General Assembly Resolution 2758. Recognition on paper is shrinking, the shadow network is expanding, and the interpretive battle over international law is turning.

title: Taiwan's Display Industry: The Shift from a Single TFT-LCD to Micro LED
description: Taiwan was once the world's second-largest panel producer and supplier in 2002; today, facing scale competition, the display industry is integrating processes, materials, equipment, and venues into a new roadmap for next-generation Micro LED.

title: Taiwan’s Drone Industry: Thunder Tiger and the Pentagon Blue UAS List
description: How a 46-year-old Taichung model plane maker became Taiwan’s sole supplier on the Pentagon Blue UAS list, anchoring Taiwan in the non-red defense supply chain.

title: Taiwan's E-Commerce and Digital Payments: Three Trade Wars on One Island
description: From Jan Hung-tze's bet on 24-hour delivery, to Shopee burning through NT$3 billion in subsidies, to Coupang's Rocket Delivery landing — twenty years of Taiwanese e-commerce is a history of 'domestic innovation disrupted by foreign capital, then disrupted again by the next wave of foreign capital.'

title: Taiwan's Education System: An Island Experiment from Exam Hell to a Maze of Diversity
description: For 30 years, Taiwan tried to dismantle the centralized examination system; the re-examination classes in Nanyang Street shrank from 48 to 3, while private tutoring centers increased by 960 after the new curriculum was implemented. How does an island repeatedly conduct social experiments between academic pressure and educational equity?

title: Taiwan's Electronic Music and Party Culture: From Underground Rave to International Stage
description: From 1990s rave culture to Road to Ultra electronic music festivals, how Taiwanese electronic music moved from the underground to the mainstream, nurturing international DJs and independent electronic labels.

title: Taiwan's Eurasian Otters: Kinmen's Lonely Island Survival and the Silent Disappearance on the Main Island
description: Taiwan's main island has had no confirmed wild Eurasian otter records since the 1980s, and the population's current status is uncertain and deeply unpromising. The 'battlefield otters' surviving only on Kinmen face simultaneous threats from habitat fragmentation, roadkill, and microplastic pollution.

title: Taiwan's Fermented Foods and Pickling Culture
description: From stinky tofu to fermented soybean curds, exploring Taiwan's unique fermentation techniques and pickling traditions

title: Taiwan's Fifth to Ninth Grade Cohorts: The 'Strawberry' Insult Has Swapped Three Generations, While the Escalator Beneath Their Feet Has Slanted
description: When the term 'Strawberry Generation' first appeared in print in 1993, it was criticizing the Fifth Grade cohort (born 1961–1970), who are now the nostalgic yogurt-drinkers of today. Over thirty years, the people being criticized have changed several times, but the label has remained unchanged. What has actually moved between these five cohorts is the 'escalator' of 'hard work pays off': it slowed down around 2002, its entrance was raised by housing prices, and then it split into two. The path relying solely on salaries has nearly stopped, while the path relying on parental capital continues to move.

title: Taiwan's FinTech Development
description: A Wall Street golden boy returns to Taiwan to launch a mobile payment platform; nine years later, the company is seized and its account balances total less than a thousand dollars. This is not just one person's story—it is the story of an entire island's decade-long tug-of-war between 'openness' and 'loss of control' in FinTech.

title: Taiwan's Fisheries Modernization: How a Fishing Net Connects Qianzhen, the Three Oceans, and the Island's Table
description: Tracing Taiwan's fisheries from coastal livelihoods to a transoceanic industry: from colonial fisheries administration and postwar Qianzhen Port's cold chain, to the 1979 distant-water development plan, the 1982 EEZ regime, and 2005 international sanctions. The article examines fisheries schools, aquaculture exports, fishing village households, port diversification, and flag-state responsibility, revealing the resource, labor, local governance, and international regulatory realities behind production growth.

title: Taiwan's Five Landforms and Geographic Structures: From Mountain Ranges to Plains
description: Explore Taiwan's unique geographic structure, from the Central Mountain Range to the western plains, and understand the island's diverse landforms

title: Taiwan's Foreign Trade and Global Supply Chains
description: From export-oriented to critical supply chain nodes: How Taiwan maintains trade advantages amid US-China confrontation

title: Taiwan's Forest Ecosystems
description: A vertical journey from sea level to the summit of Yushan, traversing the densest forest spectrum on Earth

title: Taiwan's Fuel Pricing Mechanism and CPC: The NT$36 Saved, Booked First Under the Name of a Company Standing at the Front
description: On March 22, 2026, a woman in Yunlin saved NT$36 by filling up before a price hike — the same day the Premier said people should thank CPC at the pump. From the 2008 freeze to this year’s war-driven surge, Taiwan lets this state company, at a 93% debt ratio, absorb spikes first and recoup them via supplementary budgets. Savings split evenly per liter; who benefits most has never been tallied.

title: Taiwan's Funeral Culture and Views on Death
description: From the wailing of professional mourners to the garden of Yongli Cemetery — Taiwan spent fifty years moving from burial to cremation, then another ten moving from columbaria to a spot beneath a tree.

title: Taiwan's Gaming Industry and Digital Entertainment
description: From early distributors to original developers, how Taiwan has found its voice in the global gaming market

title: Taiwan's Garbage Truck Culture: When World-Class Melodies Become Cues for Civic Society
description: From Beethoven''s "Für Elise" to Padarewski''s "A Maiden''s Prayer," the melodies echoing through Taiwan''s streets are not merely signals for waste collection—they constitute a half-century-long social experiment that has uniquely shaped global recycling rates and distinctive neighborhood cohesion.

title: Taiwan's Gig Economy Generation: Survival and Choices in Multi-Job Roles
description: When a master's degree only secures rent for a Taipei studio, gig work is not a choice—it's the math of survival.

title: Taiwan's Guai Guai Culture: How Green Snacks Became the Guardian Deity of the Tech Industry
description: From graduate students' computers to semiconductor manufacturing equipment, why do people in Taiwan believe green Guai Guai can keep machines running smoothly?

title: Taiwan's Hand-Shaken Beverage Culture
description: From bubble milk tea to premium teas, the rise and global expansion of Taiwan's hand-shaken beverage culture

title: Taiwan's Independent Bookstore Culture: How a Book Becomes a Neighborhood's Living Room
description: From the history of Chongqing South Road, Wenluotin, and Tangshan Bookstore to the micro-bookstores of Guanshan, Pinglin, Changbin, and Penghu, this article explores how Taiwan's independent bookstores have reorganized curation, local memory, migrant reading, gender issues, Indigenous culture, and community relations into public spaces amidst discount wars, digital reading, and rent pressures, while examining the real costs of subsidies, logistics, labor, and local revitalization.

title: Taiwan's Indigenous Language Revitalization Movement
description: The Thao people of Taiwan have only 4 remaining fluent speakers, yet Taiwan has become one of the world's most intensive language revitalization laboratories. From the 2017 Indigenous Languages Development Act to digital language platforms, a quiet rescue operation is accelerating.

title: Taiwan's Industrial Transformation and Upgrading: From Manufacturing Powerhouse to Innovation Powerhouse
description: Taiwan's industrial structure has shifted from labor-intensive to knowledge-intensive, with policies such as the 5+2 Industrial Innovation Plan and the Six Core Strategic Industries advancing the upgrading of traditional manufacturing and the development of emerging industries.

title: Taiwan's International Trade Policy: Seeking Positioning in the Wave of Globalization
description: In 2024, exports to Mainland China and Hong Kong dropped to 31.7%, with the United States rising to become the second-largest market. Formal FTAs are limited to Panama and Guatemala; CPTPP applications remain stalled, focusing on Taiwan-US 21st Century Trade Initiative, Taiwan-UK ETP, and the 2026 reciprocal trade agreement. This article examines how Taiwan finds a path for its export economy amid diplomatic constraints through bilateral agreements.

title: Taiwan's Island Geography: Features and Formation
description: Explore Taiwan's unique island geography, from plate tectonics to landform structures, uncovering the natural mysteries of the island of Formosa

title: Taiwan's Labeling in International Standards
description: From ISO codes to open-source software — how Taiwan's name is written, disputed, and corrected in global digital infrastructure

title: Taiwan's Letterpress Culture: How Movable Type Pressed Public Language onto Paper
description: Tracing Taiwan's letterpress history—from the Church News, Japanese-era newspapers, the Wanhua printing cluster, post-war Shanghai typefaces, and Ri Xing Type Foundry—to understand how movable type enabled the stable reproduction of vernacular Taiwanese, news, textbooks, government documents, and commercial information. It explores how lead type, fonts, artisan labor, and digital archives constitute a production technology for public language, and considers how preserving old machinery must also preserve the craft process and embodied knowledge.

title: Taiwan's Long-Term Care System Development
description: The world's most advanced long-term care system, yet shadowed by an even larger invisible caregiving ecosystem

title: Taiwan's Machine Tool Industry
description: From the Golden Corridor of Dadu Mountain to TMTS 2026: the resilience, collapse, and rebirth of Taiwan's machine tool industry, and the structural anxiety behind its 2024 fall from global 5th to 7th place.

title: Taiwan's Marine Ecology and Coral Reef Conservation
description: Surrounded by sea on all sides, Taiwan is home to rich marine ecosystems. From the coral bleaching crisis to cetacean conservation, this piece explores the protective outcomes of marine national parks and the challenges ahead.

title: Taiwan's Marine Pollution Governance and Conservation Challenges
description: Examining the current state, challenges, and innovative solutions for marine conservation in Taiwan amid marine debris, overfishing, and climate change

title: Taiwan's Mascots: From Datong Baby Gifts to Global Local Characters
description: The arrival of the Datong Baby in living rooms in 1969, the fervor ignited by the professional baseball mascots in 1990; later, Oh Bear, Xiongzan, Fish Head Boy, and Caiqi Duck brought tourism, urban governance, sports, and local cuisine onto one stage. The true test for all Taiwanese public sector bears is not how cute they look, but whether they can move beyond billboards and one-off events to perform concrete tasks for a locality.

title: Taiwan's Mask National Team: How Taiwan Connected 92 Production Lines in 40 Days
description: In 2020, when masks ran short, Taiwan assembled machine-tool makers, textile mills, the military, and government into a supply chain. In 40 days, 92 production lines came online. What matters most is the manufacturing resilience that emerges when normally competing makers collaborate under one shared deadline.

title: Taiwan's Mountains and Hiking Culture
description: 268 peaks above 3,000 meters are packed onto a single island, yet it took Taiwanese people half a century before they were allowed to freely climb their own mountains.

title: Taiwan's Music Festival Culture: Why This Island Needs So Many Outdoor Parties
description: From a stage built on a Kenting beach by two Americans in 1995, to more than 50 festivals spread across the island every year. Taiwan may have the world's highest density of music festivals — and the trailblazer wasn't Taiwanese.

title: Taiwan's Music Industry and the Streaming Era: The Transition Path from Record Stores to Digital Platforms
description: An exploration of how Taiwan's music industry navigated the crisis following the record store golden age, evolving from its proprietary subscription platform KKBOX in 2005 to today's digital ecosystem coexisting with Spotify and Apple Music.

title: Taiwan's National Scenic Area System
description: A "national-level" tourism-first experiment: how 13 scenic areas navigate between conservation and development

title: Taiwan's New Idol Generation
description: In 2020, someone bet NT$130 million on manufacturing idols in Taiwan. Four shows won four Golden Bell Awards, more than fifty people debuted — then the champion group's popularity plummeted. The hardest thing about Taiwan's idol industry has always been: what happens after you debut?

title: Taiwan's Official Website Resources: The 30-Year Miracle from 25 Sites to a Digital Powerhouse
description: In the summer of 1995, the Executive Yuan decided to participate in the World Internet Expo the following year, leading 25 central agencies and local governments to build the first government websites. Over the next three decades, Taiwan developed online tax filing, electronic official document exchange, and open government data platforms, entering the top ten of IMD's World Digital Competitiveness ranking for the first time in 2021. This article includes a list of official websites categorized by domain at the end.

title: Taiwan's Offshore Wind: From the Typhoon Trials of the Taiwan Strait to the Survival Battle of the Global Green Supply Chain
description: By the end of 2025, Taiwan’s offshore wind installed capacity surpassed 4.4GW. Facing geological challenges, adjustments in localization policies, disputes over block development tendering, and the insatiable green power hunger of global tech giants, how is this offshore green energy experiment reshaping the island’s energy lifeline?

title: Taiwan's Old Streets: Culture and Commercial Districts
description: From Qing Dynasty port prosperity to Japanese colonial Baroque mansions, Taiwan's old streets are a commoner's history written in bricks and tiles.

title: Taiwan's Open Source Spirit — The Engineers Powered by Love
description: Taiwan's most influential open source project isn't a piece of software. It's a group of engineers who showed up at a hackathon and told their government: 'You're doing it wrong. We'll do it ourselves.'

title: Taiwan's Paper Industry: From Sugarcane Bagasse Competition to Recycled Paper Circulation, How Paper Wrote an Industrial History
description: In 1917, research began on using sugarcane bagasse for papermaking; in 1935, the Zhongxing Paper Mill in Yilan commenced operations. From bagasse and imported wood pulp to calcium carbonate "stone paper," how does an island lacking self-sufficiency in pulpwood timber continue to rewrite its paper industry path?

title: Taiwan's Pastry Culture
description: From the 1877 fengyan gao (phoenix-eye cake) of Lukang's Yuzhenzhai to Chen Yao-hsun's red-soil salted egg yolk pastries that sold out in under 30 seconds, a 150-year layered story of Taiwan's pastries. In between: the square pineapple cake revolution of Yifutang during the Japanese era, Fengyuan Baquan's olive-shaped egg yolk pastry experiments, 270 hectares of contract-farmed native pineapples at the foot of Bagua Mountain, the craft breakthrough of oil-skin-wrapping-oil-flake, and century-old Han bakeries sharing the Mid-Autumn table with world bread champions.

title: Taiwan's Pigeon Racing: Letting Young Birds Fly Into a Wind Without Referees, So Everyone Has a Chance
description: Taiwan's pigeon racing merges young-bird sea racing, loft technology, private pigeon clubs, industry chains, and betting into a single rule set. This system creates an imagination of fairness where everyone has a chance by manufacturing high risk, yet it offloads the costs of disorientation, loss of contact, and post-race abandonment onto the young birds making their debut, leaving behind dilemmas in animal welfare, public governance, local society, and accountability.

title: Taiwan's Plate Tectonics and Seismic Activity
description: An exploration of Taiwan's geological characteristics, situated at the intersection of the Eurasian and Philippine Sea plates, and the reasons for its frequent seismic activity.

title: Taiwan's Political Landscape and Electoral System
description: A comprehensive analysis of Taiwan, from its constitutional structure and central/local electoral mechanisms to its deep-rooted party politics culture, showing how it maintains a vibrant and rigorously institutionalized democracy amidst complex geopolitics.

title: Taiwan's Provincial Tensions
description: Provincial tensions are not the story of two groups of people disliking each other — they are a power struggle over who has the right to define a 'Taiwanese.' They die and come back to life in the ballot box, quietly evaporate in the demolition of military dependents' villages, and yet have never truly ended.

title: Taiwan's Public Health and Epidemic Response System
description: In 2003, a botched hospital lockdown at Hoping Hospital killed 30 people. Seventeen years later, when COVID-19 swept the globe, Taiwan drew on that trauma to hold zero community transmission for 18 months. How a national wound became an island's immune memory.

title: Taiwan's Queuing: From Imposed Order to Collectively Maintained Fairness
description: In 1979, Taipei City once enshrined queuing into urban governance; queues on MRT platforms, restaurant number-calling systems, and lines before popular food stalls later transformed this bodily discipline into the fair language of everyday service. Queuing may seem like a waste of time, yet it allows strangers to share a visible set of rules.

title: Taiwan's Rainbow Road: Love and Equality from Street Protests to the 'Wei-Meng Planet'
description: The 2017 Constitutional Court Interpretation No. 748 opened the path to marriage equality in Taiwan. From Chi Chia-wei's decades of solitary advocacy, to Yeh Yung-chih's lesson in gender education, to 'Wei & Meng's' everyday sweetness — how has Taiwan's LGBTQ+ community written a new chapter of equality in Asia through love and resilience?

title: Taiwan's Religious Beliefs: An Empire of Faith Grown from Fear
description: The island with the highest temple density in the world and ranked second in Asia for religious freedom, its two largest faiths—Wangye and Mazu—have historical origins tied to plague and death. From 17th-century military migrants bringing deity statues across the Black Ditch, to the 94-point score in the 2025 Freedom Report; from the 1953 ban on Yiguandao to its legalization as the first after martial law lifted in 1987, to the four major Buddhist mountains and the Presbyterian Church each taking their own path in church-state relations—Taiwan's faith is not in scriptures, but in the incense smoke at street corners.

title: Taiwan's Reservoirs and Water Resource Management
description: From water crises to reservoir sedimentation: Taiwan's water resource challenges and regional distribution imbalances

title: Taiwan's Rice Food Culture
description: From 85 kg to 42 kg of rice consumed annually: A food revolution and cultural persistence in a rice island nation

title: Taiwan's River Systems and Hydrological Characteristics: A Hydrological Geography of Short, Rapid Flows and Seasonal Changes
description: Exploring Taiwan's unique river systems, from the Chiuanan Irrigation Canal to the Gao-Ping River, to understand how island topography shapes its hydrological features.

title: Taiwan's Robotics Industry
description: The island that leads the world in semiconductors — why is it 'making up for lost time' in the robotics era? From the 2026 unveiling of NCAIR, looking back at the miracle and blind spots of Taiwan's precision machinery.

title: Taiwan's Rural Education: What Children Lack Is Not Inspirational Stories, But an Unbroken Support System
description: Rural education is not simply 'schools in the mountains are farther away.' From teacher turnover and multi-age teaching to transportation, housing, family support, community connections, and society's singular imagination of success, the real difficulty is that the entire support system often unravels layer by layer once a child leaves the classroom.

title: Taiwan’s Salt Industry: 338 Years of Sun-Drying and How It Found a New Existence After Industrialization
description: In 1665, Chen Yonghua built salt pans at Saikou in Tainan, turning seawater, monsoons, and sunlight into an industry. Between 1952 and 1961, industrial and agricultural salt demand rose from 35,000 to 245,000 metric tons, yet salt fields faced obsolescence amid industrialization and global trade; after the last mechanical harvest in 2002, Jingzaijiao and Zhou Nan returned the landscape of cessation to local stewardship.

title: Taiwan's Same-Sex Marriage and Gender Equality
description: From outed individuals during martial law to Asia's first marriage equality law, the 33 years of petitioning, notarization, and litigation by Qi Jiawei redefined marriage in Taiwan.

title: Taiwan's Scooter Culture
description: The country with the world's highest scooter density didn't choose scooters — it never had another option. Now it's accidentally become the global laboratory for electric two-wheelers.

title: Taiwan's Seafood Culture
description: Fresh seafood delivered directly from fishing ports, seafood restaurant culture, and seafood dishes like oyster omelet showcase Taiwan's island characteristics surrounded by the sea and its rich seafood culinary traditions.

title: Taiwan's Shipbuilding Industry: Turning Fish Ponds, Sugarcane Fields, and Shallows into Maritime Industry
description: The Kaohsiung CSBC shipyard, completed ahead of schedule in 1975, rose from fish ponds, sugarcane fields, and harbor shallows to create a 1-million-ton dry dock. The 2001 restructuring came at the cost of layoffs and pay cuts, while post-2016 developments linked shipbuilding, marine engineering, and offshore wind energy. What Taiwan's shipbuilding industry truly left behind is not just ships, but a maritime industrial capacity capable of repeatedly shifting between national planning, industrial technology, and market crises.

title: Taiwan's Shoe-Off Rule: A Household Boundary Without a Genkan
description: From Japanese colonial residences to indoor slippers, schools, and cultural venues, how Taiwanese people turn a door with no fixed form into a negotiable boundary between indoors and outdoors.

title: Taiwan's SMEs and Hidden Champions: The Economic Miracle Sustained by 1.71 Million Ordinary Enterprises
description: The true backbone of Taiwan''s economy is not just the "protective shield" semiconductor giants, but 1.71 million seemingly ordinary SMEs that create 79% of all jobs, including many hidden champions dominating global niche markets.

title: Taiwan's Soundscape: Classical Music from Garbage Trucks, Birdsong on the Metro, and an Island Heard But Rarely Listened To
description: In the same year, Taipei Metro turned station music into art while removing the alarm sound melody in favor of bird calls. Sounds were simultaneously aestheticized and functionalized. These sounds that Taiwan''s Noise Control Act seeks to eliminate are, in fact, landmarks by which we identify "this is home." A question from a Master of Soundscape Studies: understanding Taiwan can begin by asking, "What sounds do we habitually ignore?"

title: Taiwan's Space Industry: A Satellite Powerhouse Without a Rocket
description: Taiwan assembles hundreds of billions in electronics for the world, yet only launched its first sub-meter resolution satellite in 2025 — a story of technological sovereignty, geopolitical reality, and a commercial space dream still in progress.

title: Taiwan's Spectrum of Sovereignty: Four Positions Plus One Status Quo, A Map of Identity Quietly Redrawn Over Thirty Years
description: In the seven days following the Trump-Xi meeting in May 2026, Lai Ching-te publicly reaffirmed Taiwan''s sovereignty twice, using three different names: "Republic of China," "Republic of China (Taiwan)," and "Taiwan." A single president compressing these three names into one statement—"all are sovereign and independent"—is a microcosm of contemporary unification debates. The percentage supporting the "status quo" rose from 9.8% in 1994 to 33.2% in 2023; the binary framework describing Taiwan is no longer sufficient.

title: Taiwan's Startup Ecosystem
description: The evolution of Taiwan's startup ecosystem, from early challenges to today's accelerators, venture capital environment, and unicorn pursuits

title: Taiwan’s Stock Market and Capital Market: From the 1990 Collapse at 10,000 Points to the World’s Sixth Largest in 2026, an Island with 44% of Its Net Worth Staked on One Stock
description: On April 28, 2026, Bloomberg flashed the headline “Taiwan Overtakes Canada.” An island whose 1990 collapse from the 10,000-point level wiped out the retirement savings of 160,000 people climbed, thirty-six years later, to become the world’s sixth-largest stock market — but of its US$4.47 trillion in market capitalization, nearly half rested on a single semiconductor company.

title: Taiwan’s Stray Animal Culture: From Twelve Nights to the Death of a Leopard Cat, the Trolley Problem of Animal Protection and Wildlife Conservation
description: In 2013, Twelve Nights moved the entire island to tears; in February 2017, Taiwan became East Asia's first zero-culling country. Eight years later, at six o'clock on the evening of May 11, 2023, a young leopard cat died in the jaws of a free-ranging cat. The Ministry of Agriculture's 2022 survey counted 159,697 free-ranging dogs nationwide, and automatic cameras operated by the Leopard Cat Association of Taiwan found dogs at 91% of leopard cat activity sites. Animal protection and wildlife conservation are not opposites. The issue is that this island still has more than a million lives with no one to take responsibility for them. This article does not take sides; it examines a question Taiwan has not yet finished answering.

title: Taiwan's Street Trees: A Road Named After a Tree, and a Century-Long Unfinished Decision
description: At No. 292, Section 2, Qiasong Road, Changhua City, the house number is named after an old Qiasong tree whose age is debated — the road was adapted to the tree, not the tree to the road. From Yasusada Tashiro''s tree-planting theory in 1898, to the widespread planting of blackboard trees in the 1980s, to over six thousand people petitioning in 2026 to ban heading-back pruning, each generation of Taiwanese has made decisions about the trees on the street. Yet that pruning guideline stating "strictly prohibited" remains merely "for reference and use by various agencies" to this day.

title: Taiwan’s Tap Water: A Century of Engineering and the Anxiety of Drought
description: In 1885, Taipei residents were already digging wells, filtering, and disinfecting water; by 2026, we still treat the tap as background noise. From the Japanese colonial-era waterways to the establishment of Taiwan Water Corporation in 1974, and through droughts, leaks, and raw water pollution, this article asks a routine yet extraordinary question: how much public engineering must a single drop of water undergo before it appears on schedule when you turn on the tap?

title: Taiwan's Teacher Discipline Dilemma: Twenty Years from the Disappearance of the Cane to Afraid to Open Their Mouths
description: In 2006, Taiwan legislated to ban corporal punishment in schools, becoming the 109th country in the world to achieve a zero-corporal-punishment status. But when the law was passed, 'corporal punishment' had no clear legal definition, and there was no accompanying disciplinary alternative plan. The result: the cane disappeared from the lectern, and teachers' confidence in discipline disappeared with it. At one end, students with ADHD were strapped to chairs with plastic zip ties; at the other, teachers chose to manage nothing at all.

title: Taiwan's Tech Storytelling: 100-Point Chips, 60-Point Microphones
description: Taiwan makes 100-point chips but tends to describe them in the voice of a supplier briefing. For the same chip, Qualcomm tells a myth and MediaTek reads out a spec sheet; NVIDIA makes none of its chips with its own hands, yet its net profit is double that of its foundry. The market worked out this 40-point gap long ago, and the bill is printed right in the net margin.

title: Taiwan's Textile Industry: From Sunset Sector to the Hidden Champion of Olympic Function Wear
description: How a traditional industry once seen as 'dying' is transforming its narrative of resilience by creating high-tech gear for global teams at the 2024 Paris Olympics, using recycled PET bottles, discarded fishing nets, and even captured factory emissions.

title: Taiwan's Tin Shed Houses: A Skyline Propped Up by 716,000 Illegal Structures
description: In August 2024, a fire at a farm machinery shop in Liujia, Tainan, trapped a family of five on the third-floor tin-roof addition; none survived. As of July 2023, Taiwan had 716,372 illegal structures, with New Taipei City adding 32,000 per year. The government announces demolitions every year—and every year another 10,000 structures appear. That layer of orange and silver metal is simultaneously Taiwan's ugliest streetscape and the most-cited legend of public safety.

title: Taiwan's Top 50 Companies: The Sacred Mountain That Holds Up One Table, and Also Holds Up a Single-Point-of-Failure State
description: On May 19, 2026, TSMC alone accounted for 31.51% of the Taiwan Capitalization Weighted Stock Index and roughly 40% of the total market capitalization of Taiwan stocks; the top 50 companies together sustain an economy the size of one GDP, but one company among them has hijacked that GDP's fate. Electronics account for 36%, finance 25%, and traditional industries 10%; the so-called tripartite balance of electronics, finance, and traditional industries is in fact half a body held up by one electronics leg. From the night Jensen Huang and Morris Chang took a photo together at Ningxia Night Market, to the 32 lives lost on Kaixuan 3rd Road before dawn, this ranking is both Taiwan's irreplaceable spine and its most fragile single point of failure.

title: Taiwan's Transitional Justice
description: Taiwan has revoked nearly six thousand convictions from the authoritarian era, yet almost no perpetrator has been held accountable—a gap that is harder to explain than the White Terror itself.

title: Taiwan's Transportation System: How an Island Compressed Itself into 90 Minutes
description: In 1946, Taiwan switched overnight from left-hand to right-hand traffic. The Central Mountain Range runs 273 km north to south, splitting 36,000 sq km of island into two halves. Sixty years later the HSR compressed 394 km into 90 minutes, and the Snow Mountain Tunnel shrank the Yilan trip from 2 hours to 40 minutes. Then came 14 million scooters jamming every intersection. This island's transportation story is its identity story.

title: Taiwan's Urban Development and the Rural-Urban Divide
description: 70 years transformed Taiwan from agricultural island to urban island: The light and shadow of six special municipalities concentrating 70% of the population

title: Taiwan's Vegetarian Culture
description: Taiwan ranks among the top three globally for vegetarian population ratio, from Buddhist vegetarian traditions to modern plant-based protein innovation

title: Taiwan's Volunteer Culture and Civic Engagement: The Daily Kindness of an Island
description: Thirty housewives saving fifty cents a day grew into a charity empire spanning 128 countries — Taiwan's volunteer culture is not a slogan, but a collective DNA written in everyday life.

title: Taiwan's Volunteer Firefighters: After Work They Put On the Uniform, Giving Localities a Second Fire Brigade
description: Called volunteers, yet they have statutory organization, professional training, operational command, and disaster insurance. From the Japanese-era fire-fighting associations to today's mountain search and rescue, this local force fills the time gap in the fire protection system while exposing challenges in recruitment, training, safety equipment, family support, and long-term retention.

title: Taiwan's VR Decade: From Cher Wang's 'Year One' to Selling the Team to Google
description: In 2016, HTC launched the Vive at MWC Barcelona and Cher Wang declared it the 'Year of VR.' Nine years later, HTC sold its XR team to Google for $250 million. What happened in between is an island's collective bet on the next big thing — and its collective loss of faith.

title: Taiwan’s White Dolphins: Legal Habitat Doesn’t Guarantee Safe Seas
description: In 2020, the western coast’s white dolphins finally gained 763 square kilometers of legally designated important habitat, yet fishing gear, ports, pollution, and underwater noise continue to compete for space in the same shallow waters.

title: Taiwan's White Terror
description: The martial law period of 1938 was not maintained by a few thousand secret agents, but by the 'collective responsibility guarantee' system where two million families across Taiwan had to vouch for each other to work, enroll in school, or get married. Chen Zhixiong, Shi Shuihuan, Gao Yisheng, and Bai Yang—four names, four reasons for arrest, one common machine.

title: Taiwan's Women's Movement: From a Magazine Published During Martial Law to Laws That Reshaped Families and Schools
description: In 1971, Hsiu-lien Lü proposed "New Feminism"; in 1982, Yuan-chen Lee and others founded *Women''s New Knowledge*; and after the 1996 murder of Wan-jui Peng, a night march was launched. All these milestones culminated in the Gender Equality Education Act, the Domestic Violence Prevention Act, and the Employment Equality Act. The history of Taiwan''s women''s movement is not merely about securing quotas for women, but about transforming harms, caregiving, and labor—originally dismissed as mere "household chores"—into public issues, thereby equipping women with institutional language for recourse in the workplace, family, and schools.

title: Taiwan's Youth Career Confusion: Sixteen Years of School, and the Most Common Sentence After Graduation Is 'I Don't Know What I Want to Do'
description: A 2006 Youth Affairs Council survey found that the three capabilities employers valued most were work attitude, stress resilience, and communication skills — but Taiwan's universities teach professional knowledge and technical skills. The Ministry of Education spent twenty years building platforms, revising indicators, and running programs; the definition of 'employability' went through four versions; and university students were still asking the same question on graduation day. The problem may never have been with the students.

title: Taiwan’s YouTuber Industry and Culture: From Tsai A-ga to Chi Hsuan, the Digital Cultural Evolution of an Island
description: How did a creator who began with magic become Taiwan's first YouTuber with ten million subscribers? Behind this milestone lies the full story of Taiwan's online video culture evolving from local entertainment into international cultural export

title: Taiwan's Yue Lao Map: Pick a Temple Before Seeking a Partner — This Island Has at Least Ten Yue Lao with Different Roles
description: When seeking romance in Taiwan, there's a premise many don't know: there isn't just one Yue Lao. Tainan's Four Great Yue Lao each handle different domains: seeking romance, seeking stability, cutting off bad romances, and seeking reconciliation. Taichung's Le Cheng Temple, a 1753 old temple, is famous for effective reconciliation. New Taipei's Wei Ming Tang's Rabbit God specializes in LGBTQ+ romance. Xiahai, Longshan Temple, and Lukang Tianhou Temple each have their specialties. The more detailed the 'partner criteria' believers write, the better — because leaving blanks gives Yue Lao loopholes to exploit.

title: Taiwanblauelster: Die blaue Gang des Stadtdschungels und ein jahrhundertelanger Kampf um genetische Reinheit
description: Mit 180.000 Stimmen gewann sie 2007 den Titel des Nationalvogels – doch hinter dem Juwel der Berge steckt eine ausgesprochen sozial-aggressive Art, berüchtigt für ihre Gruppenangriffe. Von Robert Swinhoes ersten Exemplaren 1862 bis zu den heutigen Stadtvögeln, die sich an Katzenfutter bedienen: Sie überleben dank eines kooperativen Brutsystems mit 97 % Helferquote. Eine Inselgeschichte über Überleben, familiären Zusammenhalt, genetische Verteidigung und das Zusammenleben von Mensch und Wildtier.

title: Taiwaner Unternehmen: Quanta Computer
description: Von Fabrikbränden zum globalen Laptop-König – Wie Lin Hsiu-wei ein neues Imperium für das KI-Zeitalter baute?

title: Taiwaner Unternehmen: Realtek Halbleiter
description: Die Legende von sieben Ingenieuren, die mit 2 Millionen Tael (ca. 30.000 USD) ein Unternehmen gründeten und so in jede Computer weltweit gelangten.

title: Taiwanese "Handy Dishes": The Meaning, Origin, and Signature Cuisine of Banquet Culture
description: _Tshiú-lōo-tshài_ (handy dishes) means "signature cuisine." In Neimen, Kaohsiung—where loamy soil cannot grow crops but instead raised the densest group of caterers in Taiwan—a single company hosted 25,000 banquets a year during its golden age. The final broth from one pot could take four to eight hours to perfect, and the entire village knew if it was good or not the next day.

title: Taiwanese Architecture
description: From slate houses to skyscrapers: an island's architectural journey through time

title: Taiwanese Banquet: The Feast That Goes On in Torrential Rain, and a Vanishing Tradition Spanning the Realms of Humans, Gods, and Ghosts
description: A 120-table banquet, where evening torrential rain flooded up to the calves and over a dozen trout swam about; head chef Wang Yi-yong rolled up his sleeves, waded in to catch the fish, and in the end only one was missing. For three hundred years, this is how banquets have been: if the host doesn't call it off, the feast goes on. Today this craft is at a crossroads: the dishes have entered five-star hotels and Michelin, and gained fame overseas, yet the entire body of ritual knowledge that mobilizes the whole village and spans the realms of humans, gods, and ghosts is quietly being lost for lack of successors.

title: Taiwanese Braised Food Culture: How a Pot of Dark Broth Evolved from a Preservation Technique into a Street-Side Choice
description: The rise of heated braised dishes in the 1980s and the emergence of chain brands like Beggar's Group in the 1990s transformed street stalls into replicable experiences. From Chaoshan braising techniques and soy sauce chemistry to cold versus hot consumption and cold-chain logistics, what Taiwan's braised food culture truly preserves is not a fixed recipe, but the freedom for each person to choose ingredients, flavors, and lifestyles.

title: Taiwanese Braised Pork Rice (Lurou Fan)
description: Von der Küche der Militärfamilien zum nationalen Gericht: Eine Erkundung des Nord-Süd-Konflikts und der kulturellen Identität rund um das taiwanische Braised Pork Rice.

title: Taiwanese Bread and Baking
description: From Wu Bao-chun's World Championship to 85°C's international expansion, exploring the unique charm of Taiwanese bread

title: Taiwanese Breakfast Culture: Twenty Thousand Shops Sell the Same Breakfast, Yet No One Owns It
description: In 1955, three soy milk shops lined up at Yonghe Zhongzheng Bridge; the one with the 'Yonghe Soy Milk' sign never left a trace. Seventy years later, concentrated soy milk and factory-made pastry skins tore down the barriers to opening a shop. The Judicial Yuan reclassified 'MexiMi' as a weak trademark, and an entire street sprouted Mii-Miii, Hongyi, and Morning Beautiful Rice Cake. This meal could not hold its recipe, could not hold its name, and could not hold the body standing in front of the griddle—so it became the shared dawn of twenty thousand shops.

title: Taiwanese Childhood English Names: Mary, Kevin, and the Naming Authority of Cram-School Teachers
description: From turning pages in a cram school to passport romanization to the Starbucks counter, that name was never one you chose. A history of naming that runs from Hess in 1983 and Sesame Street English''s 1987 slogan, "NO CHINESE, ENGLISH PLEASE," through the Legislative Yuan''s 2024 amendment allowing Indigenous names to appear alone, bringing the question back to that 30-second pause.

title: Taiwanese Comics
description: From Liu Hsing-chin and Ao Yu-hsiang of the 1970s “Kingdom of Comics,” to Chen Uen’s conquest of Japan in 1991 as an “Asian Treasure,” Tsai Chih-chung’s comic adaptation of classical philosophy in Zhuangzi Speaks, and then the 2010 Golden Comic Awards and the 2017 Creative Comic Collection, Taiwanese comics have passed through a downturn under the pressure of Japanese manga and are now recovering their own original voice.

title: Taiwanese Companies: Realtek Semiconductor
description: The legendary story of seven engineers who started a company with NT$2 million and sent the little crab into every computer in the world

title: Taiwanese Company: Uni-President
description: In 1967, 38-year-old Kao Chih-yuan started a small factory in Tainan with 82 employees, making flour and animal feed. More than half a century later, the company has grown from a single pack of Uni-President noodles into a retail empire of 7,248 stores—including 7-Eleven, Starbucks, RT-Mart, and Carrefour: your breakfast tea egg, midnight beef noodle soup during typhoons, and even the utility bills you pay at convenience stores are largely products of this company. How did a Tainan flour mill become the container holding a day in the life of every Taiwanese person? This is a microcosm of Taiwan's history that you walk past every day but rarely read about.

title: Taiwanese Condiments and Seasonings
description: Taiwanese specialties such as soy sauce paste, satay sauce, sweet chili sauce, and fermented bean paste form the foundation of the island's distinctive flavors, reflecting a philosophy of seasoning shaped by multicultural fusion.

title: Taiwanese Curators and the Construction of Art Culture
description: From institutional beginnings in the early 1990s to today's international platforms, how Taiwanese curators have constructed local art discourse amidst globalization and found their voice within the international biennial system. A 30-year evolution of cultural identity and professional institution-building.

title: Taiwanese Dessert Culture
description: From Yujing Mango Ice to the Snowflake Ice Revolution: Exploring Taiwan's Unique Culture of Eating Ice Even in Winter

title: Taiwanese Enterprise: Cathay Financial Holdings
description: Taiwan's largest financial holding group, a financial empire built by the Lin Yuan Group

title: Taiwanese Enterprise: Formosa Plastics Group
description: The petrochemical empire built by Taiwan's God of Management Wang Yung-ching, and the manufacturing legend of the Formosa Plastics Four Treasures

title: Taiwanese Enterprises: ASE Group
description: The world's largest OSAT provider: Why did a construction company owner pivot to semiconductors?

title: Taiwanese Enterprises: Quanta Computer
description: From factory fire to global laptop king: How Lim Pai-li built a new empire for the AI era?

title: Taiwanese Food Overview: No Dish Is Purely Taiwanese, and Every Dish Is Taiwanese to the Core
description: Beside the Chiayi Fountain roundabout in 1949, Lin Tien-shou sliced chicken, laid it over white rice, and poured Minnan-style braising sauce on top; only after the U.S. military stationed in postwar Taiwan moved into Shuishang Air Base and brought large numbers of turkeys to Taiwan did this bowl evolve from chicken rice into turkey rice. From Indigenous slate-grilled wild boar, Hakka stir-fried pork intestines with shredded ginger, and military dependents' village Sichuan-style beef noodles to bubble tea invented in Taichung in 1986, and onward to the 419 restaurants included by Michelin in 2025. This island spent four hundred years cooking every borrowed dish into its own form.

title: Taiwanese Fried Chicken (Yansuji)
description: In den 1970er Jahren begann Chen Ting-chih (陳廷智), der seine Restaurantscheiterte, in Ximending, Taipeh, mit frittierten Fleischstücken zu verkaufen. Fünfzig Jahre später ist Yansuji ein einzigartiger Snack in Taiwan, der nur einen Wagen und eine Pfanne benötigt – CNN hat ihn zweimal auf seiner Liste der Must-Eats genannt, aber die authentischste Art, ihn zu essen, ist immer noch in einem Papiersack am Straßenrand mitten in der Nacht.

title: Taiwanese Glove Puppetry (Budaixi): From Temple-Square Bans to the Palm-Held Universe of Thunderbolt Fantasy
description: On March 2, 1970, Huang Jun-hsiung's Shih Yen-wen brought Taiwan's factories to a halt and emptied classrooms, scoring a 97% TV rating; four years later the government banned it on grounds of 'disrupting normal work schedules.' This palm-held art, having endured Kominka suppression, TV bans, and the videotape revolution, finally cracked open the global anime market with Thunderbolt Fantasy.

title: Taiwanese Hakka Music: From Mountain Songs to Lin Sheng-xiang's Award Refusal and the Politics of Language
description: Hakka mountain songs originated in labor life, while Hakka eight-tone ensembles accompanied weddings and funerals. In 1999, the Labor Exchange Band won the Golden Melody Awards for Best Composer and Best Producer with *We Are Going to Sing Mountain Songs*, ushering in the era of Hakka rock. The 14th Golden Melody Awards in 2003 established the Best Hakka Vocalist category; in 2004, Hsieh Yu-wei became its first recipient. In 2007, Lin Sheng-xiang won with *Planting Trees* but refused the award on stage, calling for classification by musical genre rather than language, igniting a debate over the existence of language-based categories that led to the creation of the Golden Indie Music Awards three years later. Hakka TV, founded in 2003, has continued to expand the visibility of Hakka-language music. The threat of language loss persists, but the tension between preservation and innovation continues to drive Hakka musicians forward.

title: Taiwanese Independent Music: How a Record Store That Could Not Pay Its Staff Opened an Island's Ears
description: From the gamble of taking over Crystal Records with NT$300,000 in debt to No Party for Cao Dong selling out its first pressing in coffee shops. Thirty-five years of Taiwanese independent music is not an underdog victory story, but a long wager by a group of people determined to let unheard sounds be heard

title: Taiwanese Indigenous Ecological Wisdom and Environmental Conservation
description: Exploring the traditional ecological knowledge accumulated by Taiwan's indigenous peoples over thousands of years, and its important value and practical applications in modern environmental conservation

title: Taiwanese Instrument Manufacturing: Taiwanese Hands in the Global Soundscape
description: In the late 1940s, Zhang Lianchang, a picture framer from Houli, salvaged a burnt Japanese saxophone near a fire and welded Taiwan's first brass instrument; later, millions of guitars from Jupiter on the Nanzi line and the ticking music boxes from Otaru all passed through Taiwanese hands. This memory of a sound-making supply chain is more worthy of preservation than that of fighting heroes.

title: Taiwanese Iron Window Grilles: How a Security Grill Wields a Household's Autobiography
description: From the 1950s to the 1970s, iron window grilles spread alongside Taiwan's residential and steel supply. Originally for theft prevention, they later left the owner's profession, faith, travels, and family memories on the street facade. From the 1958 Legislative Yuan's 48-panel grille, to the residential grids of Beitun, Taichung, and the neighborhood contexts of Lukang and Anping, these iron pieces reveal how old houses simultaneously protect life and display it to the street and subsequent readers, illuminating the tension between preservation and use.

title: Taiwanese Leopard Cat Conservation
description: The phantom feline with fewer than 500 individuals left—when Taiwan's last native cat species walks to the edge of extinction

title: Taiwanese Literature during Japanese Rule
description: The development of Taiwanese literature during Japanese rule from 1895 to 1945, from classical Chinese prose to the New Literature movement, examining cultural identity and national awakening in a colonial context.

title: Taiwanese Magazines: From Free China to Benesse Kids, a Reading History of Pages Turned and Swiped Past
description: In 1960, Lei Chen was imprisoned for ten years because of Free China; in 2024, Benesse Kids, which had accompanied 1.83 million families for 35 years, ended print subscriptions; in 2025, the Chinese edition of Reader's Digest closed after 60 years in print. What Taiwanese readers once turned page by page is now swiped past one page at a time.

title: Taiwanese Market Culture: A Marketplace That Sells Not Just Vegetables, But Also Preserves Urban Memory
description: From colonial public markets and post-war population shifts to the electronic payments of Taipei City, this article explores how traditional Taiwanese markets simultaneously provide food supply, popular economy, community ties, and urban memory while searching for their next place between safety, convenience, and human connection.

title: Taiwanese Media and Press Freedom
description: From Party-State Control to the Media Wild West: The Democratization Process and Digital Transformation Challenges of Taiwanese Journalism

title: Taiwanese Military Family Village Cuisine (眷村菜)
description: The flavors of various provinces brought by the 1949 migration, from kitchens within bamboo fences to the preservation of taste after military family villages were dismantled.

title: Taiwanese Noodle Culture: A Seventy-Year Saga from US Aid Flour to National Delicacy
description: From post-war military family villages to the international stage, Taiwanese noodles have written an epic of migration and homeland memory, starting with US aid flour and fusing regional memories with local innovation.

title: Taiwanese Overseas: From Exiled Students to Silicon Valley Engineers, a Diaspora Map of Two Million
description: Taiwan still has no absentee voting. Two million overseas citizens must fly home to their household registration address for every election. From the politically exiled students of the 1960s to the FAPA lobbying organization founded in Los Angeles in 1982, to the homeward pull of Silicon Valley engineers — this is a story of identity and civic capacity in diaspora.

title: Taiwanese Photography
description: From Chang Chao-tang's 1965 pioneering of the modern photography revolution to Juan I-Jung's *People and Land* defining documentary aesthetics, Taiwanese photography records the island's stories through light and shadow.

title: Taiwanese Pop Music: The Island That Made Wedding Clothes for the World, Left in the End with Songs Others Cannot Sing
description: In 1997, Taiwan was Asia''s second-largest record market, and 80 percent of all Mandopop songs were produced here. By 2005, output value had fallen to one-quarter of its former size, the market had been overtaken by China, and even Jay Chou at his peak sold only 300,000 copies per album. When songs elsewhere can be silenced over one lyric, one flag, or one taboo, this island that lost the battle of scale turned the very question of "whether something can be sung" into its last and hardest bargaining chip.

title: Taiwanese Popcorn Chicken (鹽酥雞)
description: In 1975, a failed restaurant owner from Tainan set up a cart in Ximending and fried chicken chunks with an ancestral marinade. Fifty years later, 鹽酥雞 has become one of the few Taiwanese street foods that survives without a night market or a storefront — CNN has listed it twice as a must-eat, yet its most authentic form is always a paper bag you wait for on the roadside at midnight.

title: Taiwanese Prose: A Literary Landscape Turned by Women Writers
description: From diaspora nostalgia to native identity, from male literati to female-led literary scenes. How did the most intimate yet hardest-to-define literary form become the bearer of Taiwanese emotional memory?

title: Taiwanese Screen Scoring: From Laying Emotion Under Images to Unearthing an Island's Own Sound
description: After Millennium Mambo screened at Cannes in 2001, foreign audiences kept asking, 'Who is Lim Giong?' Taiwanese screen scoring is often described as increasingly international in scale: the Sydney Symphony Orchestra, the Oscars, Cannes. Yet its true maturation lies not in technical upgrading, but in where composers draw their materials from: from imitating Hollywood-style orchestration in the 1980s to turning back toward the yueqin, Taiwanese opera, suona funeral music, and an old melody collected from the Plains Indigenous peoples. Local sound, as it turned out, is what made this island recognizable to the world.

title: Taiwanese Sensibility: Do We Need Koreans to Like It First Before We Dare Say Our Old Houses Are Beautiful?
description: In 2008, a group in Tainan launched “Old House, New Life,” rediscovering their own old houses eleven years before Koreans coined “대만감성” for Taiwan's streetscapes. When the trend exploded via K-pop in 2024, we still reached for the government's “cultural export” framing, as if that earliest way of seeing only counted once Koreans had liked it first.

title: Taiwanese Shadow Puppetry: From Mituo, the 'Shadow Puppet Cradle,' to Kominka's Saru-Kani Gassen
description: The roots of Taiwanese shadow puppetry are in Mituo, Kaohsiung — legend says that Master A-wan, who came with Koxinga 300 years ago, left the craft in this small town. In 1937, the Kominka movement forced masters to perform Saru-Kani Gassen in Japanese, and the troupe was selected as the 'First Service Corps' and survived to this day. The Donghua Shadow Puppet Troupe, six generations strong, is the oldest family puppet theater still performing in Taiwan.

title: Taiwanese Spoken Code: From "Excuse Me" to "Pronouncing D as ''Zhu''", How Four Everyday Expressions Shape Identity
description: In Taiwan, "Excuse me" can precede a real apology; "Huh?" may seem like a lack of understanding but is a cross-linguistic dialogue repair mechanism; @ is called "Little Mouse," and D is pronounced "Zhu/Chu" when swapping exam papers. These four expressions embed politeness, misunderstanding, email syntax, and Taiwanese phonology into daily life, reminding us that a "Taiwanese accent" is not just a set of pronunciations, but a recognition method left by people living together.

title: Taiwanese Sports Development and the Olympics: A Team Called "Chinese Taipei"
description: In Montreal in 1976, Canada demanded a name change to "Taiwan," which Chiang Ching-kuo viewed as a national disgrace leading to withdrawal. In Paris in 2024, on the night Lin and Yang won the men''s doubles gold medal, the entire stadium sang the national anthem lyrics to the plum blossom flag—from the inaccessible "Taiwan" to being called Taiwan worldwide; this hat called "Chinese Taipei" carries the weight of every generation''s gold medals.

title: Taiwanese Stamps: How a Small Piece of Paper Records Regime Change and Island Memory
description: In 1888, Liu Ming-chuan established the official postal headquarters in Taipei; from then on, stamps did more than pay for letters—they captured images of the island’s regimes, wars, industries, and local lives. From the Large Dragon stamps to Taiwan Post Office covers, and from flora and fauna to indigenous cultural stamps, the small space preserves not the complete truth, but the Taiwan each era chose to make visible.

title: Taiwanese Street Food
description: A 1987 mishap at Spring Water Restaurant sent bubble tea into 60 markets worldwide. From a survival tool for Qing-era immigrants to a 400-billion-yuan industry supported by 233,000 stalls today, its success formula isn''t refinement—it''s the grassroots courage of "screw it, let''s just try."

title: Taiwanese Tea Culture
description: A small island excluded from international tea quotas, which nevertheless created a golden age for the tea industry, ultimately conquering the world with a milk tea containing "small snacks."

title: Taiwanese Traditional Arts: A Miracle Counterattack from Local Theater to Cultural Empire
description: Piexie's billion-dollar empire—how Taiwanese traditional arts transformed from local temple performances into global cultural soft power?

title: Taiwanese Traditional Chinese Orchestra Music: Island Sounds Grown on Chinese Instruments
description: The erhu and pipa that crossed the strait in 1949 were performing the Bunun people's eight-part polyphony seventy years later in Taiwan. How Taiwan's guoyue transformed from a symbol of political orthodoxy into a musical species entirely distinct from its mainland counterpart.

title: Taiwanese Variety Shows: From *Group Star Meeting* to *Kangxi Lai Le*—A Social Stage
description: In 1962, *Group Star Meeting* brought the cabaret into the living room; Taiwanese variety shows subsequently not only entertained but also began creating stars and manufacturing catchphrases, providing a shared topic for the family living room. It expanded to become a model for the Chinese-speaking world during the cable TV era before being forced to rewrite itself from a studio show to a new language on mass platforms in the streaming and short video era.

title: Taiwanese Weddings, Funerals, and Life Ceremonies
description: From the Twelve Betrothal Gifts to the culture of outdoor banquet feasts, explore how Taiwanese life ceremonies find balance between tradition and modernity

title: Taiwanese Wohnsiedlerküche (Juan-Cūn Cuisine)
description: Die Geschmacksbewahrung der verschiedenen Provinzen, die durch die große Migration von 1949 in Küchen hinter Bambuszäunen und nach dem Abbau der Wohnanlagen entstand.

title: Taiwaneses no exterior: de estudantes exilados a engenheiros do Vale do Silício, o mapa da diáspora de dois milhões de pessoas
description: Taiwan ainda não tem voto no exterior, e dois milhões de cidadãos no exterior precisam voar de volta ao seu domicílio eleitoral a cada eleição geral. Do exílio político de estudantes nos EUA nos anos 1960, à fundação da organização de lobby FAPA em Los Angeles em 1982, até o efeito de retorno dos engenheiros do Vale do Silício, esta é uma história de diáspora sobre identidade e capacidade de ação.

title: Taiwanesische Campus-Reime: Vom „ABC-Hund-beißt-Schwein“ bis „Ali-Baba-klatscht-Popo“ – generationsübergreifender Humor
description: Erkundung der jahrzehntelang auf taiwanesischen Schulhöfen mündlich überlieferten Kultur: vom frühen, Sprachverflechtungen widerspiegelnden „ABC-Hund-beißt-Schwein“ bis zu den surrealen Kettenreimen von „Omas Unterhose“ und „Ali Baba“ – Analyse, wie diese Kinderreime kollektives Gedächtnis und rebellischen Geist der Kinder tragen.

title: Taiwanesische Chorprojekte: Vom Ruhm zum Sieg in Asien
description: 1957 gründeten Lu Chuan-sheng und Gu Wei-fu die Rongxing Children's Choir und arrangierten sie aus groben ländlichen Liedern zu eleganten Chorälen. Mehr als sechs Jahrzehnte später traten die Taipeh Philharmonic auf der Bühne in Ungarn mit eigener Flagge, die Baolai Middle School's Choir gewann drei Weltmeistertitel, und die Europa Chorus gewann 55 internationale Auszeichnungen. Von der Schulgemeinschaft bis zur internationalen Profi-Ebene ist diese Melodie nicht nur eine vollständige Ökologie, sondern auch eine Geschichte der Würde unter politischer Unterdrückung.

title: Taiwanesische Filmmusik: Vom Untermalen von Bildern mit Emotionen hin zum Ausgraben des eigenen Klangs einer Insel
description: Nach der Vorführung von ‚Millennium Mambo‘ in Cannes 2001 fragten ausländische Zuschauer: ‚Wer ist Lim Giong?‘. Taiwans Filmmusik wird oft als zunehmend internationaler Standard beschrieben – Sydney Symphony Orchestra, Oscar, Cannes. Doch ihre wahre Reife liegt nicht in technischen Upgrades, sondern darin, woher die Komponisten ihre Materialien beziehen: Von der Nachahmung Hollywoods Orchestrierung in den 1980er Jahren wandten sie sich dem Yueqin, dem Gezaixi, der Suona-Bestattungsmusik und einem alten, von den Pingpu-Völkern gesammelten Lied zu. Gerade die lokalen Klänge ließen diese Insel von der Welt erkennen.

title: Taiwanesische Guoyue: Inselklänge, die auf chinesischen Instrumenten gewachsen sind
description: Erhu und Pipa, die 1949 über das Meer kamen, spielen siebzig Jahre später in Taiwan die achtstimmige Polyphonie der Bunun. Wie sich taiwanesische Guoyue vom Symbol politischer Legitimität zu einer vom Festland grundverschiedenen Musikspezies entwickelte.

title: Taiwanesische indigene zeitgenössische Kunst
description: Von traditionellem Handwerk bis zur zeitgenössischen Kreation: Erkundung, wie taiwanesische indigene Künstler auf der globalen Kunstbühne Gehör finden und den Dialog zwischen indigener Identität und zeitgenössischer Kunst neu definieren.

title: Taiwanesische Nudelkultur
description: Von Militärsiedlungen nach dem Krieg zur internationalen Bühne: Taiwanesische Nudelgerichte entstanden in siebzig Jahren aus amerikanischer Hilfsmehl, verschmolzen Provinzerinnerungen und lokale Innovationen und schrieben eine Lebensmittelepopöe der Migration und Heimat

title: Taiwanesische Sensibilität: Müssen wir erst koreanische Likes bekommen, um unsere alten Häuser schön zu finden?
description: 2008 gründete eine Gruppe in Tainan die Initiative „Old House Vitality“ und begann, ihre alten Häuser neu zu betrachten – elf Jahre bevor Koreaner mit „대만감성“ die taiwanischen Straßenszenen im Sturm eroberten. Doch als dieser Trend 2024 durch K-Pop-Kameras explodierte, verwendeten wir das Rahmenwerk „kultureller Export“ der Tourismusbehörde und des Kulturministeriums, als ob dieser ursprüngliche Blick erst von Koreanern bestätigt werden müsste, um zu zählen.

title: Taiwanesische Unternehmen: MediaTek
description: Einst als „König der Shanzhai-Handys“ verspottet, hält das Unternehmen heute einen 1,5-fach höheren Marktanteil bei Smartphone-Chips als Qualcomm.

title: Taiwanesische Varieté-Shows: Von „Stars Gathering“ bis „Kangsi Coming“ – eine soziale Bühne
description: 1962 brachte „Stars Gathering“ das Nachtclub-Entertainment ins Wohnzimmer, und taiwanesische Varieté-Shows wurden nicht nur zur Unterhaltung, sondern auch zu Sternenfabriken und Schöpfern von Schlagworten, die dem Familienwohnzimmer gemeinsame Gesprächsthemen lieferten. In der Kabel-TV-Ära blühten sie zum Vorbild der chinesischsprachigen Welt auf, wurden aber im Streaming- und Kurzvideo-Zeitalter gezwungen, sich vom Studio-Format zu einer neuen Sprache auf Nischenplattformen neu zu erfinden.

title: Taiwanische Bankett-Kultur: Ein Fest, das im Sturm stattfindet, und ein Wissen, das zwischen Menschen, Göttern und Geistern verschwindet
description: Ein Bankett mit 120 Tischen, bei dem der Abendregen bis zu den Knöcheln reicht und mehrere Forellen schwimmen. Der Küchenchef Wang Yiyong taucht in die Pfütze, um Fische zu fangen, und am Ende fehlt nur einer. Seit dreihundert Jahren ist das so: Solange der Gastgeber nicht aufhört, wird gefeiert.
